case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that before a State may irrevocably terminate parental rights, due process requires proof of its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence, and a preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: This is the federal constitutional floor that 22 M.R.S. § 4055(1)(B)(2) implements, and the Court's footnote list of conforming states already included Maine's statute.
key_cases.quote: Thus, at a parental rights termination proceeding, a near-equal allocation of risk between the parents and the State is constitutionally intolerable.

key_cases.case_name: In re Children of Matthew G.
key_cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding the court did not rest its unfitness finding impermissibly on his incarceration and denying his ineffective-assistance claim because he filed no supporting affidavit.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Maine rule for incarcerated parents: incarceration is not a standalone ground, but a parent who cannot meet the child's needs now and in the foreseeable future is unfit whatever the cause.
key_cases.quote: the court did not impermissibly consider the father's incarceration in reaching its parental unfitness determination, and therefore it did not err in finding that the father is unfit

key_cases.case_name: In re Child of Christian D.
key_cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of the father's parental rights, holding the trial court's findings satisfied M.R. Civ. P. 52(a)'s requirement of specific, independently made findings and that it properly exercised its discretion in choosing adoption over a permanency guardianship.
key_cases.relevance: This is the current statement of the Rule 52(a) specific-findings requirement in Maine termination judgments and of when a reviewing court may infer findings absent a Rule 52(b) motion.
key_cases.quote: the record supports the court's ultimate findings that termination of the father's parental rights and adoption are in the best interest of the child

key_cases.case_name: In re Child of Barni A.
key_cases.holding: The Law Court vacated termination of a mother's rights to her medically fragile child and remanded, holding that where the Department never provided the 24/7 private duty nursing to which the child was legally entitled under MaineCare and never followed up on indications that the mother has an intellectual disability, the record did not establish her unfitness by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Termination cannot rest on a parent's inability to do alone what the State was legally obligated to help her do.
key_cases.quote: We cannot assume that the mother would have been found unfit if the Department had met its legal obligations.

key_cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed terminations entered in private adoption proceedings, holding that neither due process nor equal protection requires a court in a title 18-A private termination and adoption case to order the rehabilitation and reunification services that would be available in a title 22 Department case.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Maine authority distinguishing the procedural protections owed in Department-initiated terminations from those in private termination and adoption proceedings.
key_cases.quote: In summary, the court was not constitutionally required by the Due Process Clause to order the provision of any particular services in the private adoption proceeding.

key_cases.holding: The Law Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding that incarceration gives a parent no reduced standard or 'pass' on parental responsibilities and that a parent who cannot meet the child's needs now and for the foreseeable future is unfit whatever the cause of that inability, while emphasizing that incarceration is one factor among many to be assessed case by case.
key_cases.relevance: This is the actual source of Maine's incarceration-and-unfitness rule that In re Children of Matthew G. later quotes: the cause of the parental incapacity — mental illness, substance abuse, violence, incarceration or anything else — does not change the unfitness test, which turns on the parent's ability to meet the child's needs now and in the foreseeable future.
key_cases.quote: a parent who is unable to meet his child's needs—now and for the foreseeable future—is an unfit parent whose parental rights are subject to termination.
